claims.text: Pre-exposure, as-manufactured Q235 steel has a naturally formed native oxide film on its surface.
The native oxide film is a key mediator of corrosion suppression in chloride environments at room temperature.
Elevated temperature destabilizes the native oxide film and initiates faster corrosion degradation.
A mild acid etch can remove the native oxide layer from Q235 steel.
A controlled repassivation treatment can re-establish a dense oxide layer after etching.
The continuity and integrity of the native oxide film govern its corrosion-mediating behavior.
At room temperature, an intact native oxide film limits corrosion by acting as a barrier to aggressive ions.
Elevated temperature increases defect mobility and causes microstructural changes in the oxide film.
Temperature-induced defect mobility and microstructural changes make the oxide film porous or cracked.
A porous or cracked oxide film exposes more underlying steel to corrosive species and accelerates corrosion.
Samples with intact or enhanced passivating oxide films will have lower corrosion rates than oxide-removed samples.
Intact or repassivated samples will exhibit less weight loss than oxide-removed samples.
Intact or repassivated samples will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance than oxide-removed samples.
The corrosion-behavior difference among oxide-film conditions will be more pronounced at 60°C than at approximately 25°C.
The proposed mechanism is limited to chloride-rich media at approximately 25°C and 60°C.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says elevated temperature destabilizes the intact film and makes it porous or cracked, which would tend to reduce its protective advantage, whereas the predicted outcome says the difference between intact-film and oxide-removed samples will become more pronounced at elevated temperature. No explanation is given for why a destabilized intact film should produce a larger protective contrast.
